after: ## Machine code: the only language a processor runs
alt: Three stacked levels: high-level languages such as Python, C# and Visual Basic; assembly language with mnemonics and a 1:1 match to machine code; and binary machine code from one processor’s instruction set. High-level code reaches machine code through a compiler or interpreter and assembly through an assembler, because the processor runs only machine code.
caption: Whatever the language, the processor only ever runs machine code.

alt: The high-level statement total ← price + tax becomes three assembly instructions, LOAD price, ADD tax and STORE total, and each assembly line becomes exactly one machine code instruction shown as an illustrative bit pattern. Below, machine code and assembly language are compared: both are processor-specific, but assembly uses mnemonics and must be assembled.
caption: High-level to machine code is one-to-many; assembly to machine code is exactly 1:1.

alt: One high-level source program is translated separately for processor A and processor B. An assembly program written for processor A is assembled for A but will not run on processor B, which has a different instruction set, so it must be rewritten.
caption: High-level source can be translated for any processor; assembly must be rewritten for each instruction set.

after: ## Why low-level languages are still used
alt: Advantages of low-level languages: direct control of the hardware, very efficient code and precise control of what runs. Disadvantages: harder and slower to write, harder to read, debug and maintain, and not portable. So assembly is used for embedded systems and controlling specific hardware, not for most software.
caption: Control and efficiency win for embedded systems and hardware; ease and portability win everywhere else.

alt: A compiler translates a whole high-level program into an executable file that can be run again without translating. An interpreter takes each statement in turn and carries it out by calling machine code routines within its own code, generating no machine code and no executable. An assembler converts each assembly instruction into one machine code instruction.
caption: Only the interpreter does not generate machine code: it carries out each statement with its own routines.

alt: Three cards. Interpreter for development: run statements straight away, stop at the error and test changes immediately. Compiler for distribution: an executable that runs without the translator, usually faster, without giving away source code. Assembler whenever part of a program is in assembly language, such as a routine that controls hardware.
caption: Interpreter while developing, compiler for distribution, assembler for anything in assembly language.
